summary: A response to RFC 328 objecting to two of its three proposed Telnet changes, and offering an interpretation of the Reverse Break control code. The author defends Hide-your-input as a way to simulate terminals that can suppress printing.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone says he does not want two buttons taken off a remote-control. He explains why those buttons are useful and suggests how another button should work.

subtitle: Defending terminal-emulation features in the remote-terminal protocol

tldr.problem: RFC 328 proposed removing the Hide-your-input feature from TELNET, which lets virtual terminals hide keyboard input like real terminals with print-suppression capability.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC argues the feature is essential for network users to match local terminal capabilities, and proposes that the Reverse Break code should signal end-of-message conditions.
tldr.outcome: The RFC did not persuade the standards group to retain Hide-your-input, but it documented the reasoning and use cases for the feature.

today: RFC 393 is classified as Unknown status. It remains a historical record of protocol design discussion from the early TELNET era.

sections.title: Objection to Protocol Changes
sections.content: RFC 328 proposed three changes to the TELNET protocol. This response registers objection to two of them: removing the Hide-your-input control code and removing data-type flexibility. The author, writing from Lincoln Laboratory, argues that removing these features would harm network users by denying them capabilities available on local terminals.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone said to take away two important buttons from the remote control. This person says no, we should keep them.

sections.title: Hide-your-input and Print Suppression
sections.content:
The Hide-your-input TELNET control was designed to let a virtual terminal simulate real terminals that suppress printing (for passwords and other sensitive input). When a server tells a client to hide input, it promises not to echo keystrokes. This is a special case of echo suppression where the server sends text without echoing the user's keystrokes.

The RFC proposes enhancing this by adding a byte to Hide-your-input to specify how many characters should be concealed, while still sending the No-echo control so local terminals with print-suppress hardware would not need to count.
sections.plainLanguage: The Hide button works like asking your terminal not to show what you type. Some remote systems need this feature just like real terminals do.

sections.title: Character Codes and Reverse Break
sections.content:
The RFC also argues for keeping data-type flexibility to support non-ASCII character codes like EBCDIC, since some systems at connected sites use these codes. TELNET should allow servers to support users with alternate character codes and include a code to return to ASCII.

The RFC proposes that the Break code, sent from server to user TELNET, should be interpreted as an end-of-message marker to solve problems on line-at-a-time and half-duplex terminals, signaling when output is complete even without a CR-LF sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: Different computers use different letter codes, and the remote protocol should let them switch. A special signal should tell the terminal when the server is done sending a message.

references.text: Postel, J., "Proposed TELNET Protocol Changes", RFC 328, 1972.
